title: Optimal Transport Meets t-SNE: Integrated Visualization without Batch Effects in OT-tSNE
shortTitle: Optimal Transport Meets t-SNE: Integrated Visualization without Batch Effects in OT-tSNE
abstract: Visual exploration is an integral step in understanding the structure of datasets. However, systematic variation between datasets collected under different conditions, known as batch effects, can obscure shared structure and complicate their joint visualization. Existing methods often rely on cross-batch nearest-neighbor relations to integrate the batches. Yet, these local correspondences can be unreliable for challenging cross-batch geometries. We propose optimal-transport t-SNE (OT-tSNE), which replaces nearest-neighbor-based matching with globally coupled affinities derived from entropic optimal transport. Controlled synthetic experiments demonstrated that nearest-neighbor-based methods can deteriorate, while optimal-transport affinities and OT-tSNE embeddings remain robust. Across seven real single-cell datasets, we benchmarked OT-tSNE against a broad range of integration and visualization methods and found that it achieves a Pareto-efficient trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation, and integrates batches particularly well.

title: A Framework for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification under Dataset Shift
shortTitle: A Framework for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification under Dataset Shift
abstract: Graph node quantification is the supervised learning task of estimating the prevalence of different classes within an arbitrary sample of unlabelled nodes from a graph, subject to some form of dataset shift. Existing approaches to graph node quantification typically follow the standard aggregative paradigm, i.e., they use labelled nodes from the graph to train an intermediate node classifier, and obtain an estimated class distribution for the sample by aggregating the classifier's predictions for the individual nodes and then correcting the result via some adjustment strategy that accounts for dataset shift. In this work we propose a framework for graph node quantification that does away with both node-level supervision, since its training phase only requires node samples labelled by their class distribution, and node-level predictions, since it estimates class prevalence values directly, without the need of any intermediate node classifier. The framework thus allows symmetric quantification, since (unlike in standard ``asymmetric'' quantification methods) the labelled items used for training and the unlabelled items on which predictions must be issued are of the same type (i.e., node samples). This framework (that we dub GSQ, for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification) allows building pipelines consisting of a node encoder, an embedding pooler, a prevalence predictor, and an optional post-hoc scaling step. These components can be instantiated by choosing from different trainable and reservoir-based encoders, different pooling operators, and different prediction objectives. We evaluate the GSQ framework on binary and multi-class datasets with different levels of homophily, under prior probability shift and under structural covariate shift.

title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
shortTitle: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
abstract: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.

title: BEACON: Learning Observation-Conditioned Starting Points for Guided Conditional Flow Matching in Microscopy
shortTitle: BEACON: Learning Observation-Conditioned Starting Points for Guided Conditional Flow Matching in Microscopy
abstract: Fluorescence microscopy drives much of modern life science, but accessible imaging setups often yield images degraded by out-of-focus light, limited resolution, and strong signal-dependent noise. Computational restoration can recover high-quality images from such data, enabling cheaper and faster imaging at lower light dose, provided biologically meaningful structures are preserved. Guided conditional flow matching has recently shown strong results for microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution by learning distributions of plausible restorations. However, it pairs each clean target with an independent standard Gaussian sample, so the starting point of every training path does not leverage the degraded observation. This arbitrary noise--target coupling can produce conflicting velocity targets and makes the conditional velocity field harder to learn. We present BEACON, a $BE$st-of-$K$ $A$daptive learned coupling for guided $CON$ditional flow matching, which learns an observation-conditioned base distribution. During training, a lightweight conditional noise model proposes $K$ starting points for each degraded input, and the candidate with the lowest flow-matching loss supervises both networks, while a KL term keeps the proposal close to the Gaussian prior. At inference, a single draw from the learned proposal is transported along the velocity field, requiring neither candidate selection nor the target. We evaluate BEACON on ten datasets spanning microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution against 13 baseline families. BEACON achieves the best median perception--distortion rank for every pairing of a fidelity metric (PSNR, MicroMS-SSIM) with a perceptual metric (LPIPS, FID). Code and pretrained models will be released under a permissive license.

title: Every Edit Its Own Budget: Per-Instruction Token Freezing for Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-Edit Image Editing
shortTitle: Every Edit Its Own Budget: Per-Instruction Token Freezing for Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-Edit Image Editing
abstract: Accelerating instruction-based image editing when one instruction requests several edits is challenging. Many training-free accelerators for flow-matching image editors skip tokens whose prediction has stopped changing, but decide this with a single threshold for the whole image. With several edits, such a threshold, tuned for speed, freezes small and slowly settling edits first, and requested edits disappear. We propose TIDE (Training-free Instruction-aware Drift-based Editing), which gives every instruction part its own compute budget. First, TIDE finds the region of each part in the editor's own attention by unbalanced optimal transport, without masks or external models. Second, it freezes a token once its drift is small relative to its own part and moves it along the straight path to its endpoint estimate. Third, a sparse engine computes only the remaining tokens. We prove that part-agnostic rules cannot guarantee per-part error budgets, characterize the optimal per-part threshold policy up to one tie class per part, and derive when our rule attains it. On FLUX.2 Klein, one global threshold breaks at least one edit's budget in 89% of MICE-Bench images, and TIDE drops up to 77% fewer edits at matched or higher speed (48% on MICE-Bench), a gap human raters confirm. On the many-step Klein Base, TIDE is the fastest compared method on six benchmarks (4.81-4.89x) and needs 5.3x fewer TFLOPs than vanilla, the largest saving we measure. With the same settings, it is also the fastest compared method on Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, a second model family (3.46-3.52x), and drops the fewest edits on all six benchmarks. title: Delay-Tolerant Formation Tracking for Multi-AGV Systems via Reference-Shift Coupling
shortTitle: Delay-Tolerant Formation Tracking for Multi-AGV Systems via Reference-Shift Coupling
abstract: Automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that transport a load together must keep a formation while each vehicle tracks its own reference, and they coordinate over wireless links with link-dependent, time-varying and jumping delays. We propose a cascade design for differential-drive AGVs modelled as kinematic unicycles: delayed data from the neighbours drive only a second-order filter that shifts each vehicle's own reference, and an unmodified gain-scheduled tracking law follows the shifted reference. A saturation keeps the shifted reference feasible, and the feed-forward is exact, so the tracking loop never sees the network. We prove that tracking and formation errors remain bounded for arbitrary delays and converge for every bounded delay and every directed, possibly switching, graph. We also construct a strict Lyapunov function with explicit constants and prove exponential convergence and a local input-to-state estimate with delay-independent gains. On undirected graphs, the coupling attenuates the formation error caused by persistent local errors by at least the factor lambda/(lambda+Lambda*lambda_2(L)) (leak lambda, coupling gain Lambda, algebraic connectivity lambda_2(L)), for any delay. Every inequality is verified with an event-driven, error-controlled simulation. A robustness study on a high-fidelity AGV model (drive dynamics, slip, localisation errors, clock offsets, lossy Wi-Fi) comprises 4,894 runs, including paired comparisons against tuned baselines. The cascade never failed, with latencies up to 4 s, 90% packet loss and up to 12 vehicles, whereas a direct delayed coupling failed when its gain saturated the drives. Coupling reduced the formation error after traction losses by 21-32% and after safety stops by up to 47%, at the price of tracking accuracy. Localisation bias and clock offsets, which no coupling law can observe, limit the achievable accuracy.

title: TESS: Query-Guided Temporal Event-Structured Frame Selection for Long-Video Understanding
shortTitle: TESS: Query-Guided Temporal Event-Structured Frame Selection for Long-Video Understanding
abstract: Temporal localization in long videos is challenging because brief, question-relevant events are dispersed among extensive redundant content. Limited visual budgets increase the risk of omitting these events or their temporal context, undermining reliable reasoning. Existing frame selection methods emphasize semantic relevance or temporal coverage, often overlooking the complementary evidence needed to locate related events and establish their temporal relationships. To address this limitation, we propose TESS, a training-free framework for query-guided temporal event-structured frame selection. TESS selects frames that jointly show the reference event and the event asked about, in the required temporal order. Leveraging frozen vision-language representations, TESS integrates soft temporal gating, role-aware budget allocation, and within-role redundancy suppression to preserve complementary event evidence. Extensive experiments across four long-video understanding benchmarks and three multimodal backbones demonstrate that TESS consistently outperforms the strongest compared baseline by 4.0-5.5 percentage points under a fixed frame budget. Further analyses reveal greater improvements on longer videos and robust performance under tighter visual budgets, while independent evidence annotations confirm enhanced event and temporal-relation coverage. These findings establish explicit temporal evidence organization as an effective training-free strategy for preserving event relationships and supporting efficient temporal reasoning over long videos. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TESS_code.

title: A Face Robot which Imitates Human Musculoskeletal Skin System and Its Evaluation on Basic Movement of Facial Expression
shortTitle: A Face Robot which Imitates Human Musculoskeletal Skin System and Its Evaluation on Basic Movement of Facial Expression

We then evaluate the reproducibility of individual AUs in two stages: muscle actuation without skin and actuation after the silicone skin is attached. Forty of the 47 target AUs were reproduced with the muscle components, and 30 were reproduced after skin attachment. title: On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models
shortTitle: On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/Recurrent-DLLM/

title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
shortTitle: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.

title: One Subspace Is Not Enough: LocalSubspaceAD for Training-Free Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
shortTitle: One Subspace Is Not Enough: LocalSubspaceAD for Training-Free Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
abstract: Defect-free industrial samples can vary considerably in appearance, texture, and geometry. In few-shot anomaly detection, this variability has to be modeled from only a handful of images. SubspaceAD showed that a single principal subspace of foundation-model patch features is a strong training-free model of nominal appearance. However, a single subspace has to cover all of the nominal data's variability, so a deviation that is anomalous for one semantic region can be within the nominal variability of another. We propose LocalSubspaceAD, which extends SubspaceAD from a single subspace to a mixture of subspaces, assigning each group of patches with similar features its own subspace. The set of patch-features is partitioned using k-means, one subspace is fit per cluster, and each patch is scored by the minimum of re-projection residuals over all subspaces. The proposed method requires no training and no EM refinement. On MVTec AD, VisA and Real-IAD with 1, 2 and 4 shots, it improves over a single subspace (SubspaceAD) on both evaluated backbones: by 1.2 to 1.8 points image AUROC on DINOv2, and by 1.4 to 4.4 points in image AUROC, pixel AUPR and AUPRO on DINOv3. The gains are most pronounced on objects with heterogeneous nominal appearance, such as multi-instance categories and PCBs. Ablations show that the gains stem from a finer-grained model of variability through locally oriented subspaces, rather than from the subspace offsets (cluster means). We further show that the gains do not stem from added capacity alone: the local subspaces appear to capture the structure of coherent clusters in feature space, and the model does not merely act as a compressed memory bank.

title: NRG-Twins: Pixel-Level Ground Truth for Rigidity Violations in Generated Videos
shortTitle: NRG-Twins: Pixel-Level Ground Truth for Rigidity Violations in Generated Videos
abstract: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.

title: Video Models are Excellent Motion Models
shortTitle: Video Models are Excellent Motion Models
abstract: Video foundation models have emerged as powerful generators of dynamic visual content, exhibiting remarkable capabilities in synthesizing complex actions and interactions. We argue that these models have also become excellent motion generators, with motion priors that are richer and more general than those learned by dedicated motion models. Their advantage extends beyond visual realism and is manifested in two important aspects: motion naturalness, including coherent body coordination, physical plausibility, and realistic interactions with objects and the environment; and motion scope, encompassing a much broader range of activities and semantic coherence, particularly uncommon, complex, and compound actions. To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that compares video and dedicated motion models through three complementary settings: text-only motion generation, reconstruction of video-generated motion from sparse keyframes, and video-based enrichment of motion-model outputs. By converting all outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation, we evaluate motion naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical motion characteristics, and fidelity to motion constraints. Our results suggest that video foundation models can generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. Moreover, we investigate motion-conditioned generation through loose skeletal control, finding that dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion, while video models can enrich skeletal animations using sparse motion guidance. Our findings suggest a shift in the role of specialized motion models, from generating complete animations to guiding and controlling the richer motion capabilities already embedded in video foundation models.

title: See the Answer, Learn to Embed: Learning Universal Multimodal Embeddings from Hindsight
shortTitle: See the Answer, Learn to Embed: Learning Universal Multimodal Embeddings from Hindsight
abstract: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.

title: Joule is FLOP: Optimizing Tensor-Core Kernels Beyond Latency Hiding at the GPU Power Wall
shortTitle: Joule is FLOP: Optimizing Tensor-Core Kernels Beyond Latency Hiding at the GPU Power Wall
abstract: For a tensor-core kernel whose average board power stays near the GPU's power cap, runtime is approximately the energy consumed per call divided by that cap. Data movement whose latency is hidden by computation still consumes energy; reducing this traffic can raise the sustained clock and shorten execution even without reducing cycle count. We introduce Joule, a framework that accounts for this energy-frequency coupling in tensor-kernel design and scheduling. Its cost model combines hardware event counts, physical data-path energy costs, and nonlinear voltage scaling across domains to solve for sustained frequency and runtime under a power cap. Combining the model with data-movement lower bounds across memory levels and dies yields a power-aware speed of light (PSoL) that quantifies structural and implementation gaps. This analysis guides wide-tile kernels that use the full tensor memory (TMEM) capacity on B200, with fine-grained asynchronous rotation to overlap accumulator readout with tensor-core computation. It also guides power-aware spatial and temporal tile scheduling that accounts for trade-offs among read sharing, locality, and load balance. Given measured event counts, the model achieves 0.69% mean energy prediction error on B200. Across 60 dense-layer shapes, our GEMM delivers geometric-mean speedups of 4.94%, 6.64%, and 2.12% over exhaustively selected cuBLAS algorithms on B200, H100 NVL, and RTX PRO 6000, respectively. For fused Mega-MoE on eight B200 GPUs, the resulting optimizations improve performance by 2.60% to 5.17% over the upstream DeepGEMM baseline with die-local expert weights. We will open source Joule upon publication.

title: PVWander: 3D Memory-guided Panoramic Video Wandering with Path-Facing Canonicalization
shortTitle: PVWander: 3D Memory-guided Panoramic Video Wandering with Path-Facing Canonicalization
abstract: Long-horizon panoramic video wandering aims to continuously synthesize scene-consistent $360^\circ$ observations along user-specified camera trajectories from an initial equirectangular projection (ERP) panorama. Existing panoramic video models have achieved promising results in camera-controlled generation, while recent 3D-guided approaches further provide geometric guidance for improving scene consistency. However, stable long-horizon wandering remains challenging due to diverse motion--orientation relationships and imperfect memory guidance induced by accumulated generation artifacts and depth inaccuracies. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PVWander}, a 3D-memory-guided framework that accumulates generated observations into an online point-cloud memory and reprojects it to guide subsequent generation, with two complementary designs: \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} for motion--orientation alignment and \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} for adaptive memory guidance. \textit{Path-Facing canonicalization} exploits the horizontal cyclic symmetry of ERP panoramas to uniformly align each clip's ERP orientation with its principal translation direction, yielding more consistent, forward-like relative motions while preserving the prescribed camera path. \textit{Timestep-aware gating modulation} exploits the coarse-to-fine nature of diffusion denoising to adaptively regulate reprojected memory guidance through timestep-dependent channel-wise gates, preserving its structural benefits while mitigating visual artifacts from imperfect projections. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PVWander achieves improved long-horizon generation quality, while ablations validate the effectiveness of both designs.

title: A Mesh to Remember: Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds
shortTitle: A Mesh to Remember: Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds
abstract: Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object's frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).

title: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
shortTitle: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
abstract: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.

title: ObsBridge: Observation-Grounded Conditioning for Ego Trajectory Prediction
shortTitle: ObsBridge: Observation-Grounded Conditioning for Ego Trajectory Prediction
abstract: Pedestrian forecasting from ego-view observations is challenging because occlusion, limited visibility, and tracking errors corrupt observed motion histories. Such errors are particularly consequential for autonomous robot navigation. Existing paradigms typically either impute noisy history positions before forecasting or jointly train an auxiliary history reconstruction branch. However, predictors trained on clean histories may be sensitive to residual errors in recovered histories at deployment. Meanwhile, auxiliary reconstruction still computes inter-agent interactions over raw, corrupted coordinates. We investigate conditioning future prediction on both recovered historical states and raw observation evidence, with progressive training to accommodate imperfect recovery. Building on this insight, we propose ObsBridge, a flow-based trajectory forecasting framework with observation-grounded historical bridging. Specifically, ObsBridge first employs a frozen estimator to recover historical motion from agent-relative and ego-relative positions, image-plane locations, and visibility states. During training, we introduce an agent-wise curriculum that gradually replaces clean teacher histories with complete estimated histories before context encoding. This progressively exposes the predictor to estimated histories during training. Furthermore, we design a residual geometry adapter to fuse the encoded motion with original observation evidence. We aggregate the resulting representations through social attention to condition the flow-based trajectory generator. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that ObsBridge outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On EgoTraj-TBD, it reduces minADE@20 by 6.5\% and minFDE@20 by 8.7\%. The code will be provided at https://github.com/shawnliang420/ObsBridge.

title: Which Parameters to Update? An Instance-Specific Adaptation Framework for Real-World Pansharpening
shortTitle: Which Parameters to Update? An Instance-Specific Adaptation Framework for Real-World Pansharpening
abstract: Pansharpening aims to fuse a single observed image pair, comprising a low-resolution multispectral (LRMS) image and a panchromatic (PAN) image, to obtain a high-resolution multispectral (HRMS) image. Recently, deep learning-based methods have achieved significant performance due to their strong capability of extracting nonlinear features. However, distribution shifts between training data and test images can degrade the performance of pretrained pansharpening networks, limiting their generalization in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose an instance-specific test-time adaptation framework that uses the observed PAN-LRMS pair to select and update only a subset of the pretrained network's parameters. Specifically, the framework uses cross-scoring to identify parameter groups whose updates improve reconstruction across image patches. It then updates the selected groups by minimizing a loss that combines a spectral consistency term with a newly designed spatial consistency term. Experiments show that the adapted networks perform better than their pretrained counterparts and outperform representative state-of-the-art pansharpening methods on GaoFen-2, QuickBird, and WorldView series datasets.

title: The Teacher Is Already Inside: Self-Distilling Looped Language Models Beyond Their Last Loop
shortTitle: The Teacher Is Already Inside: Self-Distilling Looped Language Models Beyond Their Last Loop
abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop is readable through the shared language-model head. Post-training them is hard. Reward-only reinforcement learning needs a verifier and learns from one sparse signal per response; spreading the reward over loops collapses the entropy of every loop; and cross-loop self-distillation, as in LoopOPD, can only teach intermediate loops, because the last loop cannot learn from its own frozen copy: the loss is zero at initialisation. We observe that a looped model already contains a policy that decodes better than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELPSD (Extrapolated-Loop Policy Self-Distillation) turns this distribution into a self-distillation target: a frozen copy of the model computes it, and the model's own last loop is distilled towards it on its own rollouts, using the exact reverse KL at every visited prefix. Teacher and student are the same model, so ELPSD needs no reward, no external teacher and no privileged context, and it leaves rollouts and decoding unchanged. We show that the objective pulls the last loop towards the base model's last loop with weight 1+w and away from the base model's first loop with weight w, and that the teacher must stay frozen, since an idealised teacher recomputed from the current model extrapolates without bound. We evaluate ELPSD on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking across five math benchmarks against the base model, GRPO, RLTT and OPSD. Without any reward, ELPSD raises the average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69 and is the best method on all five benchmarks, ahead of GRPO (62.32), which uses a verifier, and the self-distillation method OPSD (61.77), which needs reference solutions.

title: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
shortTitle: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
abstract: Parameter-efficient adaptation of a speech foundation model to dysarthric speech requires a rarely justified choice: which encoder layers to adapt. A recently proposed strategy is to probe the encoder, find where phonetic information becomes most decodable, and put the adapters there. We test that inference across two ASR models (Qwen3-ASR, Whisper-small) and two dysarthric corpora (Mandarin CDSD, English UASpeech), holding recipe and seed discipline constant. The inference fails. Measured under one pipeline rather than inherited from published figures, all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, each model's minimising layer moving no further between corpora than between probe seeds. The best adaptation band is not similarly constant: none of three natural mappings from the curve to a band -- steepest improvement, lowest band-mean error, or knee location -- recovers the best tested configuration. We do not claim no statistic of the curve could work, only that these three do not. Placement still matters, but is model- and corpus-specific. On CDSD the models disagree -- Qwen3-ASR prefers its upper third (29.88% CER, three-seed mean), Whisper-small all-block LoRA (53.56%) -- while on UASpeech neither favours the upper band. At three seeds, upper-versus-all is resolved (-1.31 pp, CI [-2.16, -0.25]) but upper-versus-middle is not (-0.83 pp, CI [-2.06, +1.86]). The two models' preferences differ as a directly tested interaction (-4.71 pp, CI [-6.17, -2.89]); we designate this the primary claim, and record that the designation was made post hoc. On Qwen3-ASR x UASpeech, adapting near the input is reliably worse than not adapting at all (+9.90 pp CER). We recommend choosing the band by a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand, not by reading it off a probe.

title: ViDM: Efficient and Order-Robust Parallel Visual Decision Making
shortTitle: ViDM: Efficient and Order-Robust Parallel Visual Decision Making
abstract: Visual decision-making demands accurate judgments and timely responses. Yet for multiple questions sharing the same visual input, autoregressive multimodal large language models generate answers token by token, accumulating sequential decoding costs as question count grows and delaying completion of the decision set. Their predictions can also vary with question order. We introduce ViDM, which transforms multi-question visual inference into parallel decisions in a single forward pass, improving both accuracy and inference efficiency. ViDM organizes shared visual context, multiple questions, and question-specific decision slots into one sequence, reusing the native language-model head to produce all answer distributions simultaneously. A Decision-Query Mask aligns each decision query's direct attention with shared context and its corresponding question, while case-balanced multi-order training strengthens robustness to question reordering. Across nine benchmarks spanning image, multi-image, and video tasks, ViDM improves Qwen3.5-4B's average accuracy from 73.49% to 77.55% while achieving 8.4x the baseline's average end-to-end throughput. On GQA, where each evaluated image has 11.4 questions on average, the end-to-end speedup reaches 20.3x. ViDM also improves mean and worst-order accuracy while reducing order-induced variation across multiple benchmarks, with further validation on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and InternVL3.5-4B.

title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
shortTitle: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
abstract: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

title: Describe, Don't Ask: Caption-Driven On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Visual Perception
shortTitle: Describe, Don't Ask: Caption-Driven On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Visual Perception
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often recognize fine-grained details more accurately in a relevant crop than in the full image. Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) methods exploit this by transferring the advantage of a crop-view teacher to a full-image student. However, their supervision relies on region-specific questions curated through an elaborate synthesis pipeline, which brings three weaknesses: (1) every region needs a question--answer pair written exclusively for it, locking training into costly QA curation that is hard to scale to unlabeled images; (2) all rollouts of a region answer the same question, so the teacher supervises only the details it asks about, leaving other visual elements in the region unsupervised; and (3) every question presupposes that its target exists, so the student becomes prone to answering even when the target is absent. In this paper, we study how to turn unlabeled images into broad visual supervision through multi-aspect self-description and privileged-view distillation, and propose CaptionOPD, which replaces tailored questions with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts, ranging from general descriptions to focused captions of parts, colors, counts, text, and layout. The rollouts of a region receive different prompts, so the teacher supervises various aspects of the region. Moreover, because caption prompts mask the model to describe what is visible instead of querying a specific target, they avoid presupposing what the region contains. Using the model itself as the crop-view teacher, CaptionOPD requires no questions, no answers, and no larger model annotations: only images and region boxes. Experiments show that, trained on the same images and regions, CaptionOPD outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks.

title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
shortTitle: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
abstract: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.

title: TDD: Target-Discrepancy Distillation for Underwater Image Enhancement
shortTitle: TDD: Target-Discrepancy Distillation for Underwater Image Enhancement
abstract: Underwater degradation changes image appearance and can compromise the semantic cues used to guide enhancement. Identifying scene content alone does not explicitly specify the appearance to recover or the input-dependent changes associated with that target. We propose target-discrepancy knowledge distillation (TDD) for underwater image enhancement, which organizes guidance around these two aspects of the same restoration problem. For each degraded-reference training pair, reference features from an underwater vision-language teacher provide target-appearance supervision, while paired feature residuals describe the observation's discrepancy relative to the same target. Both representations are jointly distilled into a lightweight guidance network that predicts them from the degraded image alone; neither the teacher nor reference images are required at inference. To align their use with their supervisory roles, we introduce progressive knowledge fusion within a multi-scale enhancement network. The estimated discrepancy first conditions spatial feature updates, after which target-appearance guidance refines the updated features and channel interactions consolidate their responses. This correction-before-refinement design lets target-guided refinement build on discrepancy-conditioned features. Experiments on six underwater benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance across full-reference and no-reference metrics. Ablations and feature visualizations analyze the contributions of the knowledge source, joint distillation, and progressive fusion.

title: BCP: A Lightweight Boundary-Controlled Framework for Online Sign Language Recognition and Translation
shortTitle: BCP: A Lightweight Boundary-Controlled Framework for Online Sign Language Recognition and Translation
abstract: Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time communication and live captioning. However, powerful pretrained offline models cannot be directly deployed in this setting, while existing online methods typically retrain the entire model on simulated streaming prefixes constructed from offline videos, incurring high costs. To address this challenge, we propose Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (BCP), a unified lightweight framework that converts pretrained offline methods into online counterparts for sign-to-gloss (S2G), sign-to-text (S2T), and sign-to-gloss-to-text (S2G2T). Specifically, BCP freezes the pretrained model and introduces a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained SLR model, without any human annotation. At inference, a Boundary-Controlled Wait-K Output Policy then decides what to commit via prefix voting, yielding adaptive burst commits while preserving the output progress of the base Wait-K schedule. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily across four offline methods show that BCP, with less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per offline method, achieves a strong quality-latency trade-off on S2T and remains competitive on S2G and S2G2T.

title: STAR: Counterfactual Dual-World Rollouts and Spatial Target Adaptive Reconstruction for Visual On-Policy Distillation
shortTitle: STAR: Counterfactual Dual-World Rollouts and Spatial Target Adaptive Reconstruction for Visual On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student rollouts using a frozen teacher that views high-resolution evidence crops. Yet our cross-scale diagnostics show that models retain over half of their full-image accuracy when local evidence is completely masked, indicating that single-image correctness does not guarantee reliance on local evidence, while the need for visual correction also varies across tokens with their spatial attention states. We propose STAR, a visual on-policy self-distillation framework combining independent counterfactual dual-world rollouts with spatial-attention-guided target reconstruction. Local image editing constructs paired worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but distinct answer-determining facts, where a shared student samples trajectories independently to expose contextual shortcuts under image-consistent prefixes. Within each world, the teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to determine the visual correction direction, while the divergence between student image attention and a teacher-centroid spatial reference adaptively controls token-wise target log-probability reconstruction. Without auxiliary attention losses or test-time tool overhead, STAR improves Qwen3.5 across scales by up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy over initialization across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD's final accuracy $4.7\times$ faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.

title: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
shortTitle: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
abstract: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

title: Progressive Reliable Supervision for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation
shortTitle: Progressive Reliable Supervision for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation
abstract: Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation (B$^2$-UniDA) aims to adapt a target model to an unlabeled target domain under arbitrary label-space relationships, while neither source data nor source-model parameters are accessible during adaptation. Under such restrictive information access, reliable target supervision is unavailable, while predictions from the black-box source model can be unreliable due to source bias and domain shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Progressive Reliable Supervision (PReS), which progressively establishes and refines reliable target supervision by coordinating complementary knowledge from the black-box source model, foundation models, and the evolving target model. PReS first identifies reliable known samples by exploiting semantic consistency under diffusion-based perturbations and cross-model consensus between the black-box source model and CLIP. It then estimates the sample-wise reliability of the two predictors and adaptively integrates their complementary predictions to construct reliable pseudo labels. The resulting supervision is exploited asymmetrically to encourage confident and discriminative predictions for reliable known samples while maintaining uncertain yet locally consistent predictions for potential unknown samples. As adaptation proceeds, the emerging target-domain knowledge is further leveraged to refine both the pseudo labels and the known/unknown sample partition, forming a closed-loop process in which supervision construction and target adaptation mutually reinforce each other. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under diverse label-space relationships demonstrate that PReS achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance under the restrictive B$^2$-UniDA setting.

title: ROVO: Robust Rotation-Only Visual Odometry for UAVs at Low and Moderate Altitudes
shortTitle: ROVO: Robust Rotation-Only Visual Odometry for UAVs at Low and Moderate Altitudes
abstract: Image noise can confound rotation and translation estimates in monocular visual navigation for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at low and moderate altitudes, where even small perturbations may cause large errors in translation direction. Inspired by angular cues in long-range visual perception, we propose rotation-only visual odometry (ROVO) for monocular aerial imagery. ROVO estimates pairwise rotations from matched images, robustly averages them over overlapping windows, and aligns consecutive windows through shared frames. By retaining only orientation in the trajectory state, it prevents uncertain landmark depth from propagating to later estimates. In trajectory simulation, sliding-window ROVO achieved a mean orientation error just 10.7% as large as that of the conventional SLAM baseline. On real flight data, ROVO achieved rotation accuracy comparable to ORB-SLAM3 and DPVO under the original Bell412 settings. title: ViTacLab: Physically Consistent Visuo-Tactile Simulation, Benchmarking, and Representation Learning for Robotic Manipulation
shortTitle: ViTacLab: Physically Consistent Visuo-Tactile Simulation, Benchmarking, and Representation Learning for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich robotic manipulation, but existing visuo-tactile simulators trade physical fidelity for scalability, and benchmarks largely focus on two-finger grippers. We present ViTacLab, a framework comprising ViTacSim, ViTacBench, and ViTacPolicy. ViTacSim uses a tri-modal tactile primitive: a global sparse contact-force lattice, a local dense force array, and tactile images. Anchored to PhysX contact-solver outputs, it corrects normal inconsistency through local stiffness alignment and reconstructs tangential forces under decoupled slip-stick regimes while preserving GPU parallelism. A joint projection preserves the sparse wrench and enforces local friction cones. ViTacBench spans parallel grippers, dexterous hands, and bimanual systems, with tasks ranging from vision-dominant to tactile-dominant regimes. ViTacPolicy aggregates variable numbers of heterogeneous tactile inputs using spatial-pose embeddings and a Transformer, and aligns force-array and tactile-image modalities through a two-stream VQ-VAE with a shared codebook. Controlled Hertzian-reference indentation and real-sensor sliding tests reduce normal and tangential force RMSE from 2.31 and 1.85 N to 0.42 and 0.53 N, respectively. Throughput reaches 2,482.9 tactile-pipeline FPS at 256 parallel environments. Simulation and real-world experiments show gains on several contact-rich tasks, while low absolute success on tactile-dominant tasks highlights the remaining difficulty of purely tactile control.

title: COHERE4D: Training-Free Dense Surface Alignment for Coherent Metric 4D Human-Scene Reconstruction
shortTitle: COHERE4D: Training-Free Dense Surface Alignment for Coherent Metric 4D Human-Scene Reconstruction
abstract: Human and scene foundation models offer complementary strengths for monocular 4D reconstruction: human models recover metric-scale body meshes but lack scene grounding, whereas scene models estimate globally consistent 3D geometry and camera motion without reliable metric scale. Crucially, both models reconstruct the same foreground human surface. Yet existing methods do not directly exploit this shared surface: lacking reliable foreground human geometry in scene reconstructions, earlier approaches either resort to sparse contact constraints or learn data-driven alignment modules that generalize poorly to out-of-distribution scenes. We present COHERE4D, a training-free framework that directly registers the human surfaces predicted by independently pretrained human and scene foundation models to reconstruct a coherent, metric 4D world. COHERE4D establishes dense, pixel-aligned 3D correspondences over the visible human surface and employs RANSAC with cross-frame consensus to suppress outliers from occlusion, background contamination, and depth noise. This formulation solves for two complementary geometric quantities: a sequence-level shared scale that calibrates scene geometry and camera motion to metric human size, and per-frame human translations that align camera-space human meshes with the scaled scene geometry to enforce spatial and temporal consistency. Across diverse backbones and benchmarks, COHERE4D substantially outperforms prior methods in human--scene alignment, metric scene and camera pose reconstruction, and global human motion estimation, adding only 4,ms/frame, enabling overall inference at up to 14 FPS.

title: CodeWAM: A Code World Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
shortTitle: CodeWAM: A Code World Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
abstract: Driving world models anticipate action consequences through representations of how the world evolves. For autonomous driving, these representations must capture both the surrounding scene and the ego vehicle's motion under a candidate plan. We propose CodeWAM, a driving world model that incorporates executable code as part of its world representation. Code represents ego dynamics by expressing how the vehicle state evolves under plan execution, while a learned visual model captures scene-dependent consequences. Executing the code produces a candidate-conditioned motion sequence, which is evaluated relative to the prior plan and recorded motion history. The resulting execution consequences and learned scene outcomes jointly represent the candidate's future, enabling the planner to assess both what a plan may lead to and how the vehicle transitions into that future. The selected plan becomes part of the next decision's execution context, linking successive choices within the model. CodeWAM achieves 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD. Further experiments demonstrate improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training, supporting executable code as a complementary representation for driving world models.

title: When Knowledge-Tracing Rankings Depend on Available History: A Source-Correction and Matched-Information Audit on ASSISTments 2009 and 2015
shortTitle: When Knowledge-Tracing Rankings Depend on Available History: A Source-Correction and Matched-Information Audit on ASSISTments 2009 and 2015
abstract: Knowledge-tracing benchmarks often compare models that have different access to a learner's previous responses. We examine how data provenance, history length, and representation affect those comparisons. First, we compare a pinned ASSISTments 2009 sequence mirror against the corrected official release. Of 4,148 learners represented in both, 817 have different ordered skill-response sequences; the mirror also contains fewer labeled events. Second, we retain earlier learner-disjoint model evaluations on the 2009 and 2015 datasets, distinguishing exploratory results from a corrective 2015 replication. Finally, we evaluate a new, nonoverlapping sample of 4,000 ASSISTments 2015 learners using three models constrained to the same one-event or 20-event prior-response window. On 20,592 test responses from 582 learners, the 20-event Brier scores were 0.17667 for count-based logistic regression, 0.17389 for an order-aware logistic model, and 0.17514 for a GRU. The GRU-minus-order-aware difference was 0.00125 (95% learner-cluster bootstrap interval [0.00008, 0.00243]); at one prior event, the corresponding difference was 0.00212 [0.00120, 0.00301]. Earlier comparisons had favored the GRU against simpler history summaries. The newer analysis instead favors a logistic comparator that represents order using the same permitted event stream. These results concern predictive performance on particular historical cohorts and model settings. They neither isolate an architectural effect nor establish generalization to contemporary classrooms.

title: X-3DComposer: Feed-Forward 3D Scene Composition with Any Assets from Any Views
shortTitle: X-3DComposer: Feed-Forward 3D Scene Composition with Any Assets from Any Views
abstract: Composing an editable 3D scene from images requires an asset for each object and a layout that places the assets. 3D generation and CAD retrieval now supply the assets, but layout still lacks a general solution: scene generation methods couple it with generation, and pose estimators handle one object at a time and need true-size CAD models, depth, or iterative refinement. We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout separately from asset generation. Given one or more images of a scene, the object masks, and an asset for each object from any source, it jointly predicts the rotation, translation, and per-axis scale of all objects in a single forward pass of about one second. The key idea is to treat objects as views: renders of the assets are processed together with the scene images by a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-$Ω$, and each object pose follows in closed form from the cameras predicted for its renders. Camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth are optional inputs. When the meshes produced by five scene generation methods are kept fixed and only their layout is replaced, the layouts of X-3DComposer are more accurate than the native layouts of these methods. Compared with the stand-alone layout model SceneMaker, it reduces the scene-level Chamfer distance by 52% on IndoorMix, our test set from six indoor datasets, and by 28% on 3D-FUTURE.

title: CoFiNav: VLM-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Semantic Navigation for Open-Ended Last-Mile UAV Delivery
shortTitle: CoFiNav: VLM-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Semantic Navigation for Open-Ended Last-Mile UAV Delivery
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) delivery is an important application of the low-altitude economy, enhancing the flexibility and accessibility of last-mile logistics. Existing UAV delivery methods generally rely on precise terminal coordinates, predefined terminal specifications, or task-specific localization procedures, limiting the scope and flexibility of delivery. As UAV logistics becomes more intelligent, open-ended semantic descriptions offer a new paradigm for specifying terminal destinations. However, conventional aerial navigation methods have limited ability to generalize to delivery scenarios that require open-vocabulary terminal navigation. To enable this broader delivery paradigm, we propose CoFiNav, a VLM-guided coarse-to-fine UAV semantic navigation framework that progressively grounds relation-defined terminal destinations through hierarchical semantic search and active 3D observation. Given a task description, a coarse prior map from OpenStreetMap (OSM), and accumulated observations, CoFiNav uses a vision-language model (VLM) to determine which unresolved entity or spatial relation should be verified next. A geometry-aware module converts the semantic observation request into feasible viewpoints using RGB images and LiDAR, while conventional motion planning handles safe execution. Experiments across multiple urban environments show that CoFiNav outperforms representative adapted baselines in success rate while requiring shorter flight paths and fewer observations.

title: Assessing Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cyber-Physical Systems
shortTitle: Assessing Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cyber-Physical Systems
abstract: As the use of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes more widespread in cyber-physical systems, it becomes increasingly important to design RL agents that are able to adapt to changes in their environments in order to maintain safety and reliability. This paper addresses the question of whether different classes of RL algorithm are more robust against forgetting previously learned behaviours, a critical issue in continual learning, in non-stationary environments. We evaluate the robustness of representative examples of three important classes of RL algorithm in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment. These are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which is a model-free on-policy algorithm, Soft-Actor-Critic (SAC), which is a model-free off-policy algorithm, and Drama, which is a model-based algorithm. The agents must learn to successfully park in four different scenarios, which are presented successively, with parking spaces oriented at varying angles. We find off-policy algorithms appear to be more robust compared to on-policy algorithms due to their use of replay, while model-based algorithms do not appear to offer any direct advantage over model-free algorithms. These experiments also highlight the additional challenges of finding robust abstractions of the environment, and oversensitivity to hyperparameters.

title: CalibTrack: Exploring Learned Heteroscedastic Covariance for Robust Multi-Camera Pedestrian Tracking
shortTitle: CalibTrack: Exploring Learned Heteroscedastic Covariance for Robust Multi-Camera Pedestrian Tracking
abstract: Analytical multi-view multi-object tracking (MV-MOT) systems rely on measurement covariance estimates to guide association, fusion, and state estimation. These covariance estimates are typically heuristic, requiring hand-tuning to the specific deployment scenario. We investigate how learned heteroscedastic measurement covariance affects calibration and robustness in analytical multi-camera tracking. To support this analysis, we introduce CalibTrack, a detector-side predictor that replaces uniform measurement covariance with per-detection covariance. We evaluate CalibTrack on the WildTrack and MultiviewX pedestrian tracking datasets with multiple analytical tracker cores, including an identity-informed GM-PHD, JIPDA, and pruned delta-GLMB filter. We additionally evaluate robustness by simulating adverse weather conditions with stable diffusion, Gaussian noise, camera browning, and camera dropout. CalibTrack improves average adverse tracking performance over confidence-scaled covariance, while producing better calibrated predictions, indicating the value of heteroscedastic covariance within analytical tracking. Comparisons with stronger heuristic covariance methods show that the benefits of learned covariance remain bounded by the quality of available observations and the downstream tracker choice. Together, these findings provide a principled exploration of learned covariance estimation and its potential for uncertainty-aware analytical tracking.

title: Déjà-VAE: Training-Free Consistent Editing with Pseudo-Invertible Encoders and Latent Back-Projection
shortTitle: Déjà-VAE: Training-Free Consistent Editing with Pseudo-Invertible Encoders and Latent Back-Projection
abstract: Consistency is essential to generative workflows: repeated processing should preserve information beyond the changes explicitly requested. In latent diffusion models, this requires stability both when moving between latent and pixel spaces and when applying successive edits. Autoencoding errors and unintended changes from the editing model can accumulate across these operations, progressively altering image structure, texture, and color. We introduce Déjà-VAE, a framework that combines exact autoencoding consistency with calibrated editing stabilization, without training or fine-tuning. Its autoencoding component converts a pretrained variational autoencoder into a surjective pseudo-invertible neural network, with a fixed gain balancing deviations from the pretrained encoder and decoder. The modified decoder $D'$ is an explicit nonlinear right inverse of the encoder $E'$, satisfying $E'(D'(z))=z$ by construction. Consequently, $D'$ is a reflexive generalized inverse: latent round trips preserve their input, up to numerical precision, and repeated image reconstruction is idempotent. To suppress editing drift, adaptive wavelet back-projection finds the closest latent to the editor's output in $\ell_2$, subject to matching the previous latent on wavelet coefficients whose changes fall below calibrated thresholds. This correction is applied once per turn, with no additional network evaluations after calibration. Together, these components support workflows that remain in latent space or interleave generation with pixel-space operations and constraints. Tests across models and editing benchmarks show less drift than stock pipelines and dedicated consistency methods.

title: MRCT: An Object-Centric Two-Layer Control Architecture for Heavy-Payload Multi-Robot Transportation
shortTitle: MRCT: An Object-Centric Two-Layer Control Architecture for Heavy-Payload Multi-Robot Transportation
abstract: Cooperative transportation of heavy payloads by heterogeneous mobile manipulators requires coordinated payload motion, force distribution, and compliant physical interaction. This paper presents MRCT, an object-centric two-layer control architecture for multi-robot transportation. At the object level, a model predictive controller (MPC) generates a coordinated contact-force reference for the payload. At the robot level, whole- body impedance control (WBIC) modules on individual robots realise the reference through a confidence-based blending of velocity-tracking and impedance torques. The blending mechanism emphasises tracking when the joint-velocity error is small and increases compliance when tracking degrades because of abrupt reference changes or physical disturbances. Simulation and hardware experiments with a heterogeneous team comprising a single-arm and a dual-arm mobile manipulator transporting a near-rated table payload demonstrate accurate object tracking, regulated contact forces, and stable payload orientation. Parameter sensitivity studies, obstacle-avoidance transportation, and step-load disturbance experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of MRCT for reliable cooperative transportation under the evaluated conditions

title: InducedTFMs: A Family of Sub-Quadratic Tabular Foundation Models Using Induced Attention
shortTitle: InducedTFMs: A Family of Sub-Quadratic Tabular Foundation Models Using Induced Attention
abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a serious competitor to gradient-boosted trees, predicting on a new table in a single forward pass by in-context learning. However, their attention is quadratic in the number of samples and features, which caps pretraining at small synthetic tables and forces inference on large ones to rely on chunking or subsampling. Row-compression models reduce the feature-wise cost, but only by discarding the cell-level representation, and remain quadratic in the number of samples. We introduce InducedTFM, which replaces both attention stages of a bidimensional TFM with the induced attention of the Set Transformer, preserving cell-level representations while making its cost linear in both samples and features. Under a training budget matched to a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation, InducedTFM matches its accuracy on TabArena and on a benchmark of larger datasets, and clearly outperforms a kernel linear-attention baseline of the same asymptotic cost. It overtakes TabICLv2 in inference time on narrow tables, reaching a 30x speed-up at 640K rows, although row compression remains preferable on wide tables.

title: An Integrated Remote Sensing and Machine Learning Framework for Mapping Hazard Associated with Leached Metals
shortTitle: An Integrated Remote Sensing and Machine Learning Framework for Mapping Hazard Associated with Leached Metals
abstract: This study integrates satellite remote sensing, groundwater monitoring, and machine learning to map leached-metal-associated hazards at four coal combustion residual (CCR) sites in Virginia, USA. Constituent-specific groundwater concentrations were expressed as Hazard Quotients (HQ) and combined into a composite Hazard Index (HI). Predictors included Sentinel-2 vegetation indices, biophysical parameters, and spatiotemporal metrics (2019-2025), alongside soil, climate, hydrology, topography, and land cover. Six supervised classifiers were evaluated using spatially separated test blocks, feature-set ablation, and leave-one-site-out testing. Higher HQ coincided with lower vegetation indices in 24 of 33 metal-site combinations near monitoring wells (sign test p = 0.007). Well HI was negatively correlated with CIRE and canopy chlorophyll content at three sites (Spearman rho as low as -0.71). Random Forest achieved within-site HI classification accuracies of 0.768-0.924 and higher-HI-class recall of 0.965-0.999. For 34 constituent-site combinations, HQ classification accuracies ranged from 0.775 to 0.989. Environmental covariates generally contributed more predictive information than vegetation features. Removing vegetation predictors did not reduce performance, and distance to the CCR unit alone performed best at one site. Zero-shot cross-site accuracy declined to 0.734-0.749, no better than the majority-class baseline. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating satellite observations and environmental data with groundwater measurements for site-calibrated spatial hazard screening. The framework identifies indirect environmental associations rather than directly detecting dissolved metals, highlighting the importance of local calibration and independent validation.

title: RecurSciBench: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement in Data-Driven Scientific Research
shortTitle: RecurSciBench: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement in Data-Driven Scientific Research
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are advancing the automation of data-driven scientific research. Recent advances in recursive self-improvement (RSI) offer the potential for these agents to continuously improve through experience, but evaluating transfer across scientific tasks requires executable, scientifically verifiable tasks and independent assessment of self-improvement gains. We introduce RecurSciBench, a scalable benchmark for evaluating RSI in data-driven scientific research. Its RecurSciPipe framework automatically constructs scientific modeling and data analysis tasks from raw datasets, with execution-based verification and scientific validity checks. RecurSciBench spans four scientific domains, multiple data modalities, and varied scientific objectives. We evaluate four RSI systems by comparing their initial and evolved states on independent tasks after evolution on source tasks, covering within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain transfer. Experiments show that the benefits of self-improvement vary across agent systems and scientific domains. Positive overall gains can coexist with regressions on individual tasks. Experience can transfer across task types and benefit other domains even without measurable gains in the source domain.

title: Analysis of Federated Graph Neural Networks for Predicting Nuclear Core Properties
shortTitle: Analysis of Federated Graph Neural Networks for Predicting Nuclear Core Properties
abstract: Federated learning has grown in popularity owing to the increasing data privacy and safety concerns. It allows multiple parties to collaboratively train a model without exchanging their raw data. As an example of highly sensitive infrastructure of national importance, nuclear reactors benefit from this approach, where---while pooling multiple large datasets from different institutions could improve machine learning solutions---the confidentiality of the datasets is paramount. In this paper, we demonstrate that a graph neural network (GNN) outperforms the convolutional neural network (CNN) baseline in a federated setting for a use case concerning nuclear reactor core optimization. The GNN architecture is better suited for the nuclear reactor geometry as, unlike the CNN, it does not require padding the cylindrical core and does not assume translation invariance. The key finding of this work is that input representation is more important than model size and complexity. More sophisticated federated algorithms were employed, but the improvements derived were of lower magnitude. Experimenting with training corpus volume led to the discovery that greater fuel inventory variance is more beneficial than arrangements of existing cases, which is a direct consequence of data heterogeneity. Going forward, focus will remain on enhancing the input and readout representation.

title: GeoVLDrive: Geometry-Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
shortTitle: GeoVLDrive: Geometry-Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) planners inherit semantic knowledge from pretrained vision-language models, but their reasoning is rarely grounded in 3D scene structure and its evolution over time. We introduce GeoVLDrive, a geometry-grounded VLA framework for 3D spatiotemporal reasoning and planning. Multi-layer features from a 3D foundation model augment the vision-language backbone through gated cross-attention. A structured latent chain of thought (CoT) organizes future scene geometry, key-agent motion, and meta-actions into ordered, separately supervised latent states. An action expert generates trajectory proposals from these states and multi-layer scene features, and ranks them using scene-grounded, interacting score tokens. We also introduce NAVSIM 3DQA to train and evaluate metric 3D spatial and motion understanding. GeoVLDrive achieves 91.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.9 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2. On NAVSIM 3DQA, the geometry-grounded backbone scores 89.2% overall, 4.6 percentage points above the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B baseline. On LingoQA, the backbone achieves 68.6% Lingo-Judge accuracy.
